claim: Children's guesses under uncertainty match the probability of each hypothesis (probability matching, about 70% for a 4:1 bag) rather than always picking the best; this is read as sampling from the posterior.
agent_test: Sample k hypotheses per problem versus argmax-only at equal tokens; compare accuracy on ambiguous-evidence tasks. Competing view: noisy maximising, pragmatic switching (a30).

claim: Preschoolers are biased toward unlikely-but-supported hypotheses (conjunctive rule), and the bias fades with age: 4y 0.92, 6-7y 0.56, 9-11y 0.60, 12-14y 0.28, adults 0.25 (confirmed from the PMC text).
schema_part: G (do not collapse to the default prior) / S3 hypothesis generation
agent_test: Give the agent ambiguous blicket evidence with and without a 'list unusual rules first' step; measure conjunctive-rule identification.

claim: Frozen LLMs show the adult disjunctive bias, not the child flexible prior, on conjunctive blicket tasks; AND rules are harder than OR rules across 8+ models (2025). In 2026 active-exploration data, strong reasoning models (gpt-5, deepseek-reasoner) reach near-perfect disjunctive accuracy and gpt-5 approaches adult conjunctive accuracy but still takes about 30-45% more tests.
agent_test: Run the text blicket game at equal tokens with and without a hypothesis-flattening step.

claim: Poor LLM performance on conjunctive rules has two causes: poor exploration and a biased reading of evidence (GX-Chen 2025). In 2026 data with the rule forms named in the prompt, gpt-5 comes close to adult accuracy and plain Sonnet 4.5 reaches 87.3% (96/110), so the evidence-reading part looks smaller for frontier reasoning models. The two causes have still not been separated for them.
schema_part: S4 test choice vs S5 evidence reading
agent_test: Feed oracle test results versus self-chosen tests; separate the two error sources.

claim: Sampling many distinct hypotheses (16 to 96) as code, giving them equal weight, and choosing the test that eliminates most removes the conjunctive-versus-disjunctive gap in the 8-object blicket task (gpt-4o). The scaffold prompt also lists the two rule forms, so sampling and form-listing are confounded. No equal-token comparison and no non-blicket task exist.
agent_test: Port to our S3/S4: N distinct hypotheses, equal weight, pick max-elimination test. Compare to plain CoT at matched tokens. Only one group has shown it.

claim: Information gain of the chosen tests correlates with final accuracy in blicket tasks (Spearman about 0.76) for LMs; in humans, successful agents prune the 32-hypothesis space faster.
agent_test: Log expected information gain per test in our agent and check correlation with final accuracy.

claim: Acting on the machine matters for adults: conjunctive object identification was 0.69 (active), 0.45 (passive observer), 0.12 (passive proposer who never sees outcomes). The handicap is largely a passive-evidence effect.
schema_part: S4 -> S5 loop (run the test, read the result)
agent_test: Compare agent that proposes tests and sees outcomes against one that only proposes; same tokens.

claim: Positive testing hides conjunctive rules, and adults often treat each task as new instead of transferring overhypotheses. Jiang and Lucas 2024 (N=212 and N=250): matched training helps disjunctive transfer (p=.017 to .051), the conjunctive matching effect is n.s., and a no-transfer model predicted interventions about as well as the hierarchical transfer model (.059 vs .055).
agent_test: Check whether our agent's test plans include multi-object tests when the first single tests are ambiguous; add cross-task rule-form prior to memory.

claim: LLMs show confirmation bias in Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery (success 6% to 78% across 11 models; falsification prompts raised discovery from 42% to 56%). In thinking-mode models the opposite-test prompt costs about 12-58% more tokens per turn and helps; in non-thinking models the effect is small or mixed. Qwen3-32B on blicket went from 0.57 to 0.86. Not matched on tokens; only open and mid-size models.
agent_test: Add a 'propose an incompatible test' instruction at equal tokens; measure incompatible-to-compatible ratio and success.

claim: Exploration is more informative when the hypothesis space is stated: children told the possible rule types had informative exploration 71% vs 32% when not told (N=85, p=.002). For LLMs, no study isolates this. Plain Sonnet 4.5 with both rule types named scored 87.3% on an extended blicket task, and the GX-Chen scaffold prompt also names the forms.
schema_part: S3 -> S4 (state hypothesis space before testing)
agent_test: Enumerate the rule forms explicitly before testing versus not; compare data-sufficiency of the tests chosen.

claim: Learning-based agents (deep RL, behaviour cloning, decision transformers) fail the blicket overhypothesis task without help; forced exploration steps raise decision-transformer reward from 0.16 to 2.06 (5 steps) and 2.37 (15 steps).
agent_test: Forced early exploration in our agent (first k steps must test) versus free choice.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Belief-contradicting evidence raises exploration in children with a stable belief; children without a stable theory behave like novelty seekers. Surprise-driven exploration needs a prior to be surprised against.
agent_test: Trigger extra tests only on prediction failure versus uniformly; needs stated prior prediction before each test.

claim: LLMs do not update beliefs like a Bayesian across rounds: off-the-shelf models mostly stop improving after round 1 (Bayesian assistant 81% final round vs far lower). Prompt-level fixes (CoT, numeric encodings, 30 rounds) failed; fine-tuning on the Bayesian model's predictions helped. A hybrid that asks the LLM for beliefs and decides outside it beats direct choice but stays below fine-tuned. Models tested were 2024-25 non-reasoning models; a code-updated belief table has not been tested.
agent_test: Externalise a numeric belief table per hypothesis and update it by rule (code), versus free-text updating; at equal tokens.

claim: Structured staged prompting (CausalCoT) improves causal question answering over vanilla GPT-4 on CLadder by 8.37 points (62.03 to 70.40; confirmed in the paper text); on an earlier GPT-4 run the gain was 2.36.
agent_test: Staged causal prompt (graph, query type, formalise, solve) versus plain CoT; note gain varies by model version.

claim: LLMs are near or below random at deciding causal validity from correlation statements (Corr2Cause, 207,972 samples, best zero-shot F1 33.38 vs random 20.38), and fine-tuned models collapse under paraphrase.
schema_part: S5 (do not trust verbal causal inference from stats)
agent_test: Use a program (conditional independence test) rather than the LLM for statistical-structure questions.

claim: LLMs do well at knowledge-based causal tasks (pairwise direction 97%, counterfactual 92%, necessary/sufficient 86%) but fail unpredictably and do not use the numerical data.
schema_part: S2/S3 (use knowledge for priors, not data inference)
agent_test: Use LLM for prior proposal and data tools for likelihood; compare against LLM doing both.

claim: GPT-3 passes simple blicket and intervention vignettes but fails when seeing vs doing must be separated in causal chains, and small adversarial changes break it. LaMDA scored lowest on causal reasoning (1.34 of 5) among task families.
agent_test: Test current model on seeing-versus-doing vignettes; old-model results may not transfer to 2026 models.

claim: Children are better than LLMs at inventing novel tool uses (85.2% children vs GPT-4 75.9%) while LLMs match on familiar uses (GPT-4 83.3%); adults 95.7% on novel.
agent_test: Not a direct test of our schema; use as ceiling reference.

claim: Sequential Monte Carlo over natural-language hypotheses with an LLM proposal plus expected-information-gain experiment choice beats a ReAct-style agent in Zendo (6.55 vs 4.60 of 8; human 5.26). Choosing the experiment by code-computed information gain beat LLM-chosen (6.55 vs 4.72) and random (5.84). Uncertainty-aware question selection (UoT) raises success by 38.1% on average.
agent_test: Our S3/S4 with explicit candidate set and EIG ranking versus free question asking at equal tokens.

claim: Giving LLM agents prior information did not reliably help experimental design in BoxingGym; models often did better without it. The cause named is an overly strong early assumption that is not revised. BoxingGym measures prediction error and expected-information regret, not test diversity, so anchoring of test diversity is not shown.
agent_test: Run tests with and without stated priors; check anchoring.

claim: Developmental replications: screening-off and backward blocking replicate in most cells (2018 replication N=90: 5 of 6 comparable cells matched the Sobel 2004 originals, n=16 per cell; one 4-year-old cell was 96% vs the original 63%, p=.03). Beaton and Benton 2024 (26 four- and 33 five-year-olds) find 4-year-olds block only after additivity training. Children also split into subgroups, so group means hide variability.
agent_test: None direct; implies report per-item variance for agent tests too.

claim: Diagnostic inference in the blicket paradigm replicates but is modest: 4-5y and 6-7y at chance (about 33%), 8-10y above chance (55-60% Exp 1; 59-71% Exp 2); transfer to category membership fails.
agent_test: None; boundary on the 'preschoolers are Bayesian' reading.

claim: The strong claim that children are rational Bayesian learners is contested: Bayesian models are flexible enough to fit post hoc, and competing explanations (noisy maximising, pragmatic switching) exist.
agent_test: Use Bayesian structure as a design tool, not as a claim about mechanism.

claim: In-context learning can be framed as latent-concept inference, which supports prompting that exposes a concept or hypothesis space.
agent_test: Weak support only; theory on synthetic data.

claim: Backward-blocking and screening-off pass rates in the founding Sobel 2004 study (n=16 per age cell): indirect screening-off B 100% at 3y and 4y; backward blocking 50% (3y), 88% (4y Exp1), 63% (4y Exp2). Gopnik 2001 and Kushnir and Gopnik 2005 pass rates were not obtained.
agent_test: None; sets effect sizes for children.

claim: Blocking by itself does not show causal knowledge: preschoolers blocked equally when cues were causes or effects (N=33 and 25), while adults differed (F(1,56)=6.37). Whether 4-year-olds block depends on training on how effects add (N=26) and fits an associative model better than a Bayesian one.
agent_test: When the agent discounts a variable, check that its answer flips under a cause/effect swap.

claim: Naming the possible rule forms in the prompt is a cheap candidate fix for the conjunctive handicap: plain Sonnet 4.5 reached 87.3% on an extended blicket task with both rule types named, and the GX-Chen scaffold prompt also names them. No study tests listing forms against not listing them for LLMs.
agent_test: Run an A/B of form-listing vs none vs sampling at equal tokens.

claim: A forced falsifying test per cycle costs tokens: 12-58% more tokens per turn in thinking models (Qwen3-8B 1088 to 1716, Qwen3-32B 1030 to 1450), with small or mixed effects in non-thinking models. Not tested outside rule-discovery games.
agent_test: Add the falsify step to debugging tests and log tokens per cycle.

claim: Choosing the next test by a code-computed information-gain score beats asking the LLM to choose (6.55 vs 4.72 of 8 on Zendo) and beats random choice (5.84).
agent_test: Compute test scores in code over a hypothesis list; compare to LLM-chosen tests.

claim: No independent reproduction of the 2025 LLM conjunctive-bias finding was found. All blicket-LLM papers located (GX-Chen, Samiei, Jhaveri) share authors or lab links; Alderete 2026 (separate group) used blickets for a different aim.
agent_test: Run our own conjunctive/disjunctive test on a current model before relying on the effect.

claim: Transfer of a learned rule form to the next task helps when forms match and costs when they differ, mainly for disjunctive transfer, but many people behave as if each task is new. As agent memory this is plausible but untested on LLM agents.
agent_test: Store the last rule form as a soft prior that a surprise resets.
